paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.52:2 Rule 10.52(3)(a)(i)—“other than an order for the payment of money” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. I think that it is plain that the intention of the drafter of R. 703(a) was to exclude from the scope of civil contempt any disobedience of an order for the payment of money, and that an order to pay maintenance in fixed amounts is “an order for the payment of money” within the meaning of R. 703(a). Craft v. Craft (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 223 (Q.B.), at 225, per D.C. McDonald J. In Dickie v. Dickie, 2007 SCC 8, 2007 CarswellOnt 606, [2007] 1 S.C.R. 346, the Court considered, among other things, Rule 60.11(1) of the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, which reads as follows: A contempt order to enforce an order requiring a person to do an act, other than the payment of money, or to abstain from doing an act, may be obtained only on motion to a judge in the proceeding in which the order to be enforced was made. A motions court ordered Mr. Dickie to pay support payments, and ordered him to secure those obligations by providing an irrevocable letter of credit and posting security for costs. When he did not do so, he was found to be in contempt. That finding of contempt was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal (Laskin J.A. dissenting) (see: (2006) 206 O.A.C. 257 (C.A.)). The Supreme Court of Canada allowed the appeal and reinstated the finding of contempt. With respect to the submission that the order to post a letter of credit was really an order to pay money, the Supreme Court of Canada said, at paragraph 7, that it was “in substantial agreement with the reasons of Laskin, J.A.” Laskin J.A. said, at paragraph 104 (O.A.C.): I accept that an irrevocable letter of credit is “money or money's worth,“and that an order to post security for costs ordinarily is satisfied by the payment of money. However, to determine whether an order is an order for the payment of money under r. 60.11(1), one must consider to whom the money is being paid and the effect of the order for payment. Where money is ordered to be paid not to the creditor but into court—or its functional equivalent, to a solicitor to be held in trust—and where the effect of the order is not to create a fixed debt obligation but to secure a debt obligation, then the order is not an order for the payment of money under r. 60.11(1). In Mella v. 336239 Alberta Ltd., 2016 ABCA 226, 2016 CarswellAlta 1409, Mella was a judgment debtor of 336239 Alberta Ltd. (operating as “Dave's Diesel”). Dave's Diesel obtained an attachment order “directing [Mella] to limit their monthly expenditures … and to provide detailed monthly expenditure records”. Mella was found in contempt of that order “because he had unlawfully used more money than permitted and had failed to provide adequate expenditure records” (the first contempt order). Mella was subsequently found in contempt (the second contempt order) for continuing contempt under the first contempt order, and for evading lawful enforcement proceedings. The Court of Queen's Bench imposed monetary sanctions (a payment to Dave's Diesel equal to what was spent in contravention of the attachment order, payment of two fines, and payment of Dave's Diesel solicitor-client costs). The contempt under the second contempt order was not purged and Mella was imprisoned. Mella sought a stay of the second contempt order. One of the grounds for the stay application was that failure to pay money is not contempt. In dismissing the stay application, Schutz, J.A. said: 22 … fines imposed for contempt of court are an obligation owing to the court, separate from the civil action in which it arises: SNC-Lavalin Profac Inc v Sankar, 2009 ONCA 97 at paras 14-17, 94 OR (3d) 236; Sussex Group Ltd v 3933938 Canada Inc., 2003 CanLII 49334 at para 13 (Ont SC). Sometimes, it is appropriate to direct payment of fines for contempt to other than the Clerk of the Court: MEL(P) v BJL, 2013 ABQB 227, 560 AR 165; Berube v Wingrowich, 2003 ABQB 805, 24 Alta LR (4th) 398; Alberta Treasury Branches v Chocolaterie Bernard Callebaut Partnership, 2012 ABQB 245. 23 Two types of judgments or orders direct a person to pay money: those which direct a person to pay money to another person and those which direct a person to pay money into court. 24 It is not Mella's failure to pay his civil debt to Dave's Diesel that underlies the contempt sanctions imposed; rather, his misconduct in continuing to flagrantly breach the court's orders is the reason contempt sanctions have been imposed. The First Contempt Order found that Mella had defied a court-ordered injunction prohibiting him from exceeding a stipulated expenditure limit on household expenditures, and he had also failed to provide ordered financial records. 25 Rule 10.52(3)(a)(i) refers only to the payment of money. But, the rule does not exclude the use of the contempt power to punish Mella for defiance of, and to coerce his compliance with, a mandatory injunction explicitly limiting his household expenditures and requiring a proper accounting, nor does it preclude disgorgement as sanction. It is not determinative that the First Contempt Order requires that money or money's worth be paid because a court order that punishes and coerces is not the functional equivalent of payment by Mella to Dave's Diesel for ordinary debts—a critical distinction: Dickie v Dickie (2006), 78 OR (3d) 1 at para 103, 262 DLR (4th) 622 at paras 105–116 (Laskin JA), affd 2007 SCC 8, [2007] 1 SCR 346. Moreover, the First Contempt Order subsists unencumbered by appeal or variation. 26 Rule 10.53 expressly authorizes the imposition of fines, imprisonment and costs. 27 Fines and imprisonment are means of enforcing “compliance with the process of the court itself”: Johnson v Schwalm, 2006 CanLII 13771 at para 24, 2006 CarswellOnt 2620. Mella's imprisonment serves both as punishment and an incentive to purge his ongoing contempt: Korea Data Systems Co v Chiang, 2007 ONCA 529 at para 11, 77 CPC (6th) 253. 28 Apart from arguing that the court below miscalculated cumulative amounts owing, and mis-characterized the nature of some payments he did make, Mella does not challenge the court's extant authority to levy fines, or to make imprisonment a sanction for civil contempt. Mella has not demonstrated any error by the court below in its calculations, or characterizations, or in imposing monetary sanctions. 29 As for costs, sound public policy underlies the imposition of a costs order: it is the contemnors who ought to bear a substantial portion of the costs directly relating to their contempt, as this brings home the seriousness of their action and their responsibility for the consequences of their contempt: Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2005 ABCA 185 at para 11, 371 AR 11. As defined in the Rules of Court, a “costs award” includes “the amount payable by one party to another in accordance with … r 10.31”, and can form part of a penalty for contempt of court: Richards v Richards, 2013 ABQB 484 at para 147, 568 AR 302.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.52:3 Sloppy Practice Is Not Contempt See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Miller v. 32807 Alberta Ltd. (1986), 70 A.R. 303 (C.A.), the defendant had failed to provide adequate responses to undertakings given at discovery (as required by an order). At p. 304 the court said: Material before the learned chambers judge was, to say the least, skimpy There were responses given to the underakings. The plaintiff (respondent) considered those responses to be inadequate in the sense that “clarification” was required. Reviewing the material before the chambers judge it would be impossible to say whether the order had been complied with. We are told that the chambers judge expressed grave concern about the failure of the defendant's solicitor to respond to the correspondence about the clarification. Those facts would not, however, justify this order on this notice of motion. Striking out a defence and permitting a default judgment is a drastic remedy, for what is, is reality, sloppy and unacceptable practice as distinct from contempt.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.52:4 Rule 10.52(3)(a)(vi)—Implied undertakings See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Jutte v. Jutte (2007), 77 Alta. L.R. (4th) 126 (Alta. Q.B.), Brooker J. found that the plaintiff's lawyer (Mr. Sproule) had breached his implied undertaking of confidentiality arising from an examination for discovery. In declining to find that the breach constituted contempt of court, his Lordship said, at p. 138: 41 The foregoing cases demonstrate that knowledge of the existence of the court order that has allegedly been breached is a necessary precondition to a finding of contempt, although it may not always be necessary to prove that the defaulter intended to breach the order. 42 In this case, having regard to my previous findings, I am satisfied that the implied undertaking exists and that Sproule breached the implied undertaking. His defence is that he was not aware of the implied undertaking. His counsel argues that the implied undertaking rule is not found in the Alberta Rules of Court nor the Alberta Evidence Act, R.S.A. 2000 c. A-18. While that may be so, I note that the genesis of the rule is certainly found in the Alberta Code of Professional Conduct as referred to earlier. Does ignorance an of the implied undertaking provide a reasonable excuse for the breach? 43 With some reluctance, I hold that it does. The essence of contempt is deliberate conduct in breach of a court order or undertaking. Obviously, if someone is to be found guilty of breach of a court order, it must be shown that the offender had knowledge of that order. How else could he be expected to govern his conduct accordingly? This is no doubt why the courts are vigilant in proceedings to hold someone in contempt of a court order to ensure that there is adequate proof that the respondent has been properly served with the order. With respect to proceedings for breach of a specific undertaking to the court, one would expect the applicant to begin by proving that the respondent had given the undertaking that he has allegedly breached. By doing so, the respondent's knowledge of the existence of the undertaking is proved. 44 However, with respect to the implied undertaking here, Sproule has not given anything specifically to the court. Rather, he is presumed, as a matter of law, to have given it. He specifically denies knowing of the existence of the implied undertaking. Is that a reasonable excuse for its breach? Given the potential serious consequences which can flow from a finding of contempt of court I hold that it is. Sloppy practice is not contempt of court: Miller v. 32807 Alberta Ltd. (1986), 70 A.R. 303 (C.A.).

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.53 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) Every person declared to be in civil contempt of Court is liable to any one or more of the following penalties or sanctions in the discretion of a judge: (a) imprisonment until the person has purged the person's contempt; (b) imprisonment for not more than 2 years; (c) a fine and, in default of paying the fine, imprisonment for not more than 6 months; (d) if the person is a party to an action, application or proceeding, an order that (i) all or part of a commencement document, affidavit or pleading be struck out, (ii) an action or an application be stayed, (iii) a claim, action, defence, application or proceeding be dismissed, or judgment be entered or an order be made, or (iv) a record or evidence be prohibited from being used or entered in an application, proceeding or at trial. (2) The Court may also make a costs award against a person declared to be in civil contempt of Court. (3) If a person declared to be in civil contempt of Court purges the person's contempt, the Court may waive or suspend any penalty or sanction. (4) The judge who imposed a penalty or sanction for civil contempt may, on notice to the person concerned, increase, vary or remit the penalty or sanction.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.53:1 Rule 10.53 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.53. 1. New Rule is Essentially the same as the Old Rule In Koerner v. Capital Health Authority, 2011 ABQB 191, 2011 CarswellAlta 456; affirmed 2011 CarswellAlta 2079 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused 2012 CarswellAlta 724 (S.C.C.), Madam Justice Shelley said, at paragraph 46: 46 R. 10.53 of the Rules of Court outlines the penalties available to a court for civil contempt. It is essentially the same as the penalties set out in Rule 704 of the old Rules. … 2. Factors to Consider … any kind of negligence (advertent or inadvertent, by ommission or commission) is less blameworthy than deliberate defiance of a court order. Reliance upon (mistaken) legal advice has been recognized by some cases as a mitigating factor, when sentence is imposed … Furthermore, where the contempt consists of some type of failure to give discovery, a host of cases say that the object of the exercise is to secure the discovery, more than to punish. Severe punishments, such as summary dismissal, or striking out a defence, have been later remitted after belated compliance, in a number of cases. And any kind of attempt to purge the contempt, or to apologize, is relevant. Michel v. Lafrentz (1998), 68 Alta. L.R. (3d) 140 (C.A.), at 146, per Côté J.A. In Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v. Wenzel (2005), 48 Alta. L.R. (4th) 250 (C.A.), Fraser C.J.A., speaking for the panel, set aside a $5000 penalty assessed against a party found to be in contempt by not producing documents which had been ordered to be produced. At p. 252, Her Ladyship said: In terms of the sanction for contempt, we are of the view that the amount ordered is not adequate for its purpose. Requiring those in contempt to pay a part only of thrown-away costs related directly to the contempt does not bring home to the contemnors the seriousness of their actions and their responsibilities for the consequences attributable to that contempt. There is a public policy aspect to this entire issue. Generally, in principle, those who are found in civil contempt ought, at a minimum, to be required to accept responsibility for a substantial portion of the costs directly related to that contempt. It may be that a judge would also consider it appropriate to impose further monetary penalties or other sanctions, whether including striking of pleadings, drawing of adverse inferences, etc. In the context of this case, it is open to the case management judge in assessing the sanctions which should be imposed to take into account a number of considerations including: (1) the role of counsel, including the extent to which the actions of the respondents' counsel might have contributed to the respondents' contempt; (2) the motivation for the destruction/erasure of the computer records while the undertakings to produce them remained extant; (3) the consequences flowing from the destruction of those records and what redress should flow from that, including consideration of whether any adverse inferences should be drawn as a result thereof; (4) the entire context and history of the litigation; (5) the amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred; (6) the nature of the contempt; and (7) the degree of culpability of the contemnors. The matter was returned to chamber judge for reconsideration of the appropriate penalty. Greckol J. awarded the plaintiffs their thrown-away costs in the amount of $136,146.27 plus GST. She also ordered production of the missing information, in default of which the defendants were fined $75,000. [See: (2006), 399 A.R. 166 (Alta. Q.B.)] In McDonald Estate, Re, 2013 ABQB 602, 3 CarswellAlta 2002, 573 A.R. 1, Justice Mahoney reviewed the factors to be considered when determining the appropriate penalty for contempt. Where, however, the order relates to a child the court is (or should be) adamant upon its due observance (cf. the recent case of Corcoran v. Corcoran, [[1950] 1 All E.R. 495]). Such an order is made in the interests of the welfare of the child and the court will not tolerate any interference with or disregard of its decisions upon these matters. Least of all will the court permit disobedience of an order that a child shall not be removed outside its jurisdiction. The reason for this is obvious. The court cannot exercise its quasi-parental powers in relation to a child unless effect can be given to its orders, and it cannot enforce its orders if the child is taken abroad. In the same case Lord Denning said at p. 424: It is a strong thing for a court to refuse to hear a party to a cause and it is only to be justified by grave considerations of public policy. It is a step which a court will only take when the contempt itself impedes the course of justice and there is no other effective means of securing his compliance … Applying this principle I am of opinion that the facts that a party to a cause has disobeyed an order of the court is not of itself a bar to his being heard, but if his disobedience is such that, so long as it continues, it impedes the course of justice in the cause, by making it more difficult for the court to ascertain the truth or to enforce the orders which it may make, then the court may in its discretion refuse to hear him until the impediment is removed or good reason is shown why it should not be removed. These principles have been accepted in Canada in the cases cited by the respondent. We agree with them. F. (E.) v. S. (J.S.) (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 401 (C.A.), at 403, per curiam. In Broda v. Broda (2004), 346 A.R. 376 (C.A.), a husband in a family law proceeding was ordered (by way of a consent order) to produce certain documents by a specified date. He failed to do so, and was found in contempt. He appealed that contempt finding on the grounds that he had a reasonable excuse: he had underestimated the time he would need to produce the documents given the other things he had to do in his life. As the Court of Appeal noted (at p. 379–380): The husband advances many reasons to justify his delay, including time spent on construction of an office building, acting on his own behalf in his divorce action, and exercising access. Moreover, he submits that the statements could not be completed without providing further material to the accountant, and there had been no time to do this. In short, the husband argues that, at worst, he was guilty of not properly estimating the time within which the documents should be produced. As such, he says that he had a reasonable excuse for not producing the documents and that the mens rea requirement for a finding of civil contempt was not met. In rejecting that line of reasoning and upholding the finding of contempt, the Court said, at p. 380: In Michel v. Lafrentz et al. (1998), 219 A.R. 192, 179 W.A.C. 192, 1998 ABCA 231, at para. 21, Côté, J.A., cites a number of previous cases to support his finding that intent to disobey the court is not a necessary requirement for a finding of contempt: “[w]here someone is ordered by the court to do something, he or she must use a sufficient degree of diligence to perform, or to have the act performed.” This same principle was espoused recently by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Topgro Greenhouses Ltd. et al. v. Houweling (2003), 184 B.C.A.C. 118, 302 W.A.C. 118, 2003 BCCA 355, at para. 6, where Smith, J.A., citing R. v. Perkins, [1980] 4 W.W.R. 763 (B.C. C.A.), stated: To knowingly breach a court order is to commit a contempt of court. All that is necessary to establish the contempt is proof of deliberate conduct that has the effect of contravening the order; an intent to bring the court into disrepute or to interfere with the due course of justice or with the lawful process of the court is not an essential element of civil contempt. Of course, civil contempt proceedings have serious consequences and a criminal element to them. Sometimes, even where the necessary elements are made out, making such a finding may be inappropriate in the circumstances. For example, where noncompliance is due to circumstances beyond the control of the party alleged to be in contempt: Metaxas et al. v. Ship Galaxias et al. (No. 2), [1989] 1 F.C. 386, 19 F.T.R. 108 (T.D.). That is not the case here. Here the husband made elective choices as to how to spend his time. The time limits he breached were his own. It was a consent order that he breached. … 12. Can One Seek the Assistance of the Court When Still In Contempt? In Phillips v. Phillips (2005), 56 Alta. L.R. (4th) 26 (C.A. [In Chambers]), O'Leary J.A. (In Chambers) raised, without deciding, the question of whether the applicant before him who was seeking a stay of proceedings could ask for such assistance when she was still in contempt of court orders. At p. 30, his Lordship said: Although I do not base my decision on this point, and it was not fully addressed in argument, I question whether a person who is in contempt of court for failure to obey specific orders of the Court of Queen's Bench is entitled to the assistance of this Court. The orders she has failed to obey are those under appeal and it is suggested she may succeed in her appeals and the contempt will then cease. I do not agree with that suggestion. Unless the applicant has complied with the orders and thus purged her contempt, or has been specifically excused from compliance, she remains in contempt. In any event, the applicant is in contempt of the courts in the State of Washington in proceedings related to these. There is authority for the proposition that a court will not assist a person in contempt of its orders: F. (E.) v. S. (J.S.) (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 401 (Alta. C.A.), Horrey v. Litterst (1995), 32 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 (Alta. C.A.). 13. When Does a Court become Functus in Contempt Proceedings? In Braun Estate (Trustee of) v. Braun (2006), 55 Alta. L.R. (4th) 18 (C.A.), Ms. Braun was the subject of a receiving order which required her to file an affidavit setting out monies received and paid by either her or her company. She failed to file the affidavit within the time stipulated, and she also failed to attend examinations properly scheduled by counsel for the trustee in bankruptcy. She was found to be in civil contempt, and when she failed to purge her contempt, she was sentenced (on August 23, 2004) to 14 days' imprisonment. She continued to refuse to comply with the court's orders, and, on October 20, 2004, was sentenced to a 4-month term of imprisonment. On February 16, 2005, Ms. Braun again appeared before the court and advised that she still would not comply with the orders. Her counsel submitted that the earlier determinate sentence of 4 months' imprisonment (which had been served) rendered the Court functus and that the Court could impose no further sanction for the contempt. The matter was put over to March 11, 2005, for decision. The learned justice disagreed with defence counsel, and “held that the Court of Queen's Bench was not without jurisdiction to impose further sanctions with respect to ‘[Braun's] ongoing contempt regarding Orders of this Court.’” Ms. Braun was found to still be in contempt, and was sentenced to another 4-month term of imprisonment (referred to by the Court of Appeal as “sixth Murray order”). The March 11, 2005, order was the subject of this appeal. Berger J.A., speaking for the panel, allowed the accused's appeal, and held that the lower court was functus when it imposed the sentence on March 11, 2005. At pp. 26–27, his Lordship said: The gravamen of the analysis, I suggest, is to ascertain whether (using the criminal law analogy) the impugned act amounts to a new actus reus. A person who is in possession of stolen property over a period of five days is not subject to prosecution for five offences. On the other hand, five bank robberies will attract five charges. The same is true of contempt. Where there is a subsequent breach of a court order stemming from a positive act on the part of the contemnor, such as the breach of a restraining order or a breach of an injunction, the subsequent breach can found a second contempt charge resulting in further sanctions: Skeena Kraft Ltd. v. Pulp & Paper Workers of Canada, supra, and U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General) (1990), 104 A.R. 246 (Alta. C.A.); affirmed [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901 (S.C.C.). On the other hand, if an individual is ordered to attend examinations and wilfully fails to do so, the contempt crystallizes at the moment of non-compliance. Like possession of stolen property, nonattendance the following day does not constitute a new actus reus. If the contempt is not purged, the gravity of disobedience in the context of all of the circumstances is readily ascertained. This includes an assessment of the contemnor's motives for non-compliance, the impact on interested third parties, the public nature of the contempt and its implications for the integrity of the administration of justice. In such circumstances, one way of proceeding would be to adjourn once a finding of contempt is made and to schedule a sentencing hearing at some future date. This would allow the contemnor to consider whether to purge her contempt. If the contemnor elects to purge, that may be a mitigating factor. If the contempt is not purged, continued disobedience is neither an aggravating feature nor a fresh transgression. The sentence imposed should assume continued non-compliance. The nature of the contempt will have been assessed and will have been the subject of judicial pronouncement and sanction. Of course, it is always open to a contemnor to thereafter purge her contempt and to thereby mitigate the punishment that has been imposed. The Court, in my opinion, retains jurisdiction to reduce a fine or a term of imprisonment already imposed when a contemnor later elects to comply with the Court's order. The Court is not functus. Rule 704(4) and the common law preserve the Court's ability, in appropriate circumstances, to vary or remit the sanction. By proceeding in this fashion, respect for the administration of justice is enhanced, certainty is restored, and compliance with court orders is encouraged. Of course, the present restrained and measured practices of the Courts will continue. Judges who find a party to an action in civil contempt will almost always first consider non-penal sanctions such as the striking of pleadings and the imposition of costs. That said, if a penal sanction such as imprisonment or a fine is imposed, the judicial arsenal is not thereby depleted. The Court retains control over its own process and, if the unpurged contempt affects the fair adjudication of the suit, non-penal sanctions may still be invoked. Conclusion For the reasons set out above, I am of the view that the determinate sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the Appellant on October 20, 2004, brought the contempt proceedings to an end. The appeal from the “sixth Murray order” is allowed and that order is vacated. 14. Purging contempt In Lymer (Re), 2020 ABQB 157, 2020 CarswellAlta 398, 11 Alta. L.R. (7th) 157 (Registrar in Bankruptcy), the Registrar (L.A. Smart), gave this guidance as to when a person purges his or her contempt: A. — Purging Contempt (i)—The Test [29] A court may set aside a contempt order where “the contemnor subsequently complies with the order or otherwise purges his or her contempt”: Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, [2015] 2 SCR 79 at para 66 [Carey]. Rule 10.53(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 provides that the Court may waive or suspend penalty or sanction “[i]f a person declared to be in civil contempt of Court purges the person's contempt.” [30] It is the party seeking to purge their contempt who bears the onus of demonstrating on a balance of probabilities that they have done so: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 23, 29; Korea Data Systems Co v Chiang, 2009 ONCA 3 at paras 50–52 [Chiang]. The contemnor must satisfy the Court that they have subsequently complied with the order they previously breached to the full extent that they are reasonably able: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 24, 29; Lymer (Re), 2018 ABQB 859 at para 157; Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd, 2007 ABQB 745 at para 37 [Turkawski I]. (ii)—Principles [31] The objectives and principles that govern the contempt power are relevant to determining whether a party held in contempt has subsequently purged that contempt. [32] It is vital for a court to be able to enforce compliance with its orders: “The rule of law is directly dependent on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect” (Carey at para 30, citing United Nurses of Alberta v Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 SCR 901 at 931, 1992 CanLII 99). A civil contempt order has as its main purpose coercion—to promote compliance with a court's orders (Chiang at para 117; Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2017 ABQB 256 at paras 54, 82 [Demb ABQB 2017], aff'd 2017 ABCA 340 [Demb ABCA 2017], citing Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42 at para 59). This power, however, is one that courts must use “cautiously and with great restraint” (Carey at para 36, citing TG Industries Ltd v Williams, 2001 NSCA 105 at para 32). As such, a judge may decline to make a finding in contempt where the alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with a court order (Carey at para 37). [33] However, it is also important to recognize that, as stated by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Knapp v Munro, 2015 ONSC 5444 at para 16: Notwithstanding the court's reluctance to exercise it contempt powers, it is important that such powers be exercised in appropriate cases to ensure that parties … understand that court orders cannot be ignored or disobeyed, and that compliance with a court order is neither an option nor a bargaining chip. [34] A court assessing whether a party has purged their contempt should also consider the context of the original contempt order and the circumstances of the overarching litigation (see e.g. Turkawski I; Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd, 2008 ABQB 27 at paras 4-5, 15 [Turkawski II]; Keephills Aggregate Co v Riverview Properties Inc., 2008 ABQB 540 at para 18 [Keephills]; Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5-6). … [37] It may be possible for a party found in contempt to purge their contempt without achieving perfect compliance with the order they previously breached. This may be the case where the party shows that they are unable—as opposed to unwilling—to satisfy elements of the earlier order (Turkawski I at para 37; Turkawski II at para 15). Additionally, the court may take into consideration that “the passage of time, and other factors, may affect the true importance of receiving complete satisfaction” of an earlier undertaking or requirement (Turkawski I at para 32). The fact that a party has not achieved perfect compliance with an earlier requirement may be less important where the intended product of that requirement is no longer relevant (Turkawski I at para 53). [38] Similarly, when document production is at the heart of the earlier contempt finding, a court may consider whether production has “run its course” at the time that a party applies to purge its contempt (Demb ABCA 2017 at para 6). … [45] The party seeking to purge its contempt holds the burden of showing that they have complied with the court order they previously breached or that despite their reasonable efforts, they are unable to do so: Turkawski I at para 37; Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 24, 29. It is not enough to show merely that any outstanding obligations are extremely difficult or onerous: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at para 27. However, context is an important consideration: see e.g. Turkawski I; Turkawski II at paras 4–5 15; Kee hills at para 18; Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5–6

New Rule is Essentially the same as the Old Rule In Koerner v.

Capital Health Authority, 2011 ABQB 191, 2011 CarswellAlta 456; affirmed 2011 CarswellAlta 2079 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused 2012 CarswellAlta 724 (S.C.C.), Madam Justice Shelley said, at paragraph 46: 46 R.
10.53 of the Rules of Court outlines the penalties available to a court for civil contempt.
It is essentially the same as the penalties set out in Rule 704 of the old Rules. … 2.
Factors to Consider … any kind of negligence (advertent or inadvertent, by ommission or commission) is less blameworthy than deliberate defiance of a court order.
Reliance upon

(mistaken) legal advice has been recognized by some cases as a mitigating factor, when sentence is imposed … Furthermore, where the contempt consists of some type of failure to give discovery, a host of cases say that the object of the exercise is to secure the discovery, more than to punish.
Severe punishments, such as summary dismissal, or striking out a defence, have been later remitted after belated compliance, in a number of cases.
And any kind of attempt to purge the contempt, or to apologize, is relevant.
Michel v.
Lafrentz (1998), 68 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 140 (C.A.), at 146, per Côté J.A.
In Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel (2005), 48 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 250 (C.A.), Fraser C.J.A., speaking for the panel, set aside a $5000 penalty assessed against a party found to be in contempt by not producing documents which had been ordered to be produced.
At p.
252, Her Ladyship said: In terms of the sanction for contempt, we are of the view that the amount ordered is not adequate for its purpose.

Requiring those in contempt to pay a part only of thrown-away costs related directly to the contempt does not bring home to the contemnors the seriousness of their actions and their responsibilities for the consequences attributable to that contempt.
There is a public policy aspect to this entire issue.
Generally, in principle, those who are found in civil contempt ought, at a minimum, to be required to accept responsibility for a substantial portion of the costs directly related to that contempt.
It may be that a judge would also consider it appropriate to impose further monetary penalties or other sanctions, whether including striking of pleadings, drawing of adverse inferences, etc.
In the context of this case, it is open to the case management judge in assessing the sanctions which should be imposed to take into account a number of considerations including:
(1) the role of counsel, including the extent to which the actions of the respondents' counsel might have contributed to the respondents' contempt
(2) the motivation for the destruction/erasure of the computer records while the undertakings to produce them remained extant

(3) the consequences flowing from the destruction of those records and what redress should flow from that, including consideration of whether any adverse inferences should be drawn as a result thereof
(4) the entire context and history of the litigation
(5) the amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred
(6) the nature of the contempt; and
(7) the degree of culpability of the contemnors.
The matter was returned to chamber judge for reconsideration of the appropriate penalty.
Greckol J. awarded the plaintiffs their thrown-away costs in the amount of $136,146.27 plus GST.
She also ordered production of the missing information, in default of which the defendants were fined $75,000.
166 (Alta.
Q.B.)] In McDonald Estate, Re, 2013 ABQB 602, 3 CarswellAlta 2002, 573 A.R.
1, Justice Mahoney reviewed the factors to be considered when determining the appropriate penalty for contempt.
He said at paragraph 28: 28 As Justice Gates stated in his written reasons when dealing with Ms.

Gusa's contempt in the related estate matter before him (McDonald Estate, 2012 ABQB 704, 552 AR 308 at para 55) there is a list of factors to be taken into consideration in determining the penalty for contempt such as:
(1) whether there was deliberate defiance of a court order or whether there was an inadvertent failure to comply with the court order
(2) the role of legal counsel
(3) where there has been a failure to give discovery, the object of the exercise is more to secure the discovery rather than to punish
(4) attempts to purge contempt or to apologize are relevant
(5) the entire context in the history of the litigation
(6) the amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred
(7) the nature of the contempt; and
(8) the degree of culpability of the contemnor.
In Precision Forest Industries Ltd. v.
Cox, 2013 ABQB 524, 2013 CarswellAlta 1772, 574 A.R.

Justice Lee set out the following factors to be considered (at paragraphs 55-56): 55 In addition to the nature of the contemptuous conduct, in determining the appropriate remedy in response to a finding of contempt for breach of a court order, the court may consider factors including: a. whether the contemnor has admitted the breach; b. whether the contemnor has tendered a formal apology to the court; c. whether the breach was a single act of part of an ongoing pattern of conduct; d. whether the breach occurred with the full knowledge and understanding that it was a breach rather than as a result of a mistake or understanding; e. the extent to which the conduct of the contemnor displayed defiance; f. whether the order was a private one, affecting only the parties to the suit of whether come public benefit lay at the root of the order; g. the need for specific and general deterrence; and h. the ability of the contemnor to pay. i. the sanction of contempt should be proportional to the personal responsibility of the person in contempt and to the seriousness of the contempt.
56 In the case of breach of Court Orders which prevents an opposing party from defending an action, it may be appropriate to strike the pleading, but even this should be done on a gradual basis.
This type of escalating response is found in for example my decision of S.W. v.
K.T., 2005 ABQB 298 where fines and double fines were first imposed because the Plaintiff was unresponsive and contradictory with respect to Answers to the Undertakings, similar to the present case.
The Plaintiffs in S.W. were forced to go directly to trial and had to live with their answers.
Similarly Kevin Cox is now stuck with his answers to the Questioning until trial, which could prove to be a major problem for him.
In Demb v.

Valhalla Group Ltd., 2015 ABCA 29, in concurring with the other two Court of Appeal justices in dismissing an appeal from a case management judge's order finding that the defendants were not in contempt, Justice O'Ferrall said that a finding of contempt can have deterrence as its objective.
His Lordship said: 38 As the majority correctly points out, the appropriate standard of review demands deference to the case management judge's exercise of discretion.
Furthermore, it appears that the case management judge may not yet be finished with respect to the issue of contempt.
The order appealed from required the respondents to provide yet another further and better affidavit by September 10, 2013, and two of the respondents failed to file the required affidavit.
On the hearing of this appeal, we were advised that a second contempt application had been made to the case management judge.
It was adjourned pending this appeal.
39 Although we must defer, I question the respondents' sincerity when it comes to complying with the Rules of Court or with the orders of the Master and the case management judge.
The respondents appear to have adopted an attitude of “Let's see how little disclosure we can get away with”.
Also, their delays in complying appear to be of their own making.
This is not a case where the difficulty in complying with the Rules is disproportionate to the likely benefit.
Nor does it appear there are any remaining unresolved issues with respect to the relevancy and materiality of the documents sought.
40 It appears the case management judge adopted the approach that contempt proceedings are designed to compel compliance rather that to punish and fashioned his order with this in mind.

While the case management judge was certainly entitled to adopt that approach, there are occasions when it is appropriate to grant contempt orders that have as their object denunciation and deterrence (both specific and general).

That is, the sanctions prescribed in Division 4 of Part 10 of the Rules of Court for contravening the Rules and disobeying court orders may be employed to secure compliance; but they also may be employed to denounce and deter such behaviour, communicating to the broader legal community that the court will not accept non-compliance and disobedience as a litigation tactic.

41 Counsel for the appellant quite correctly characterizes repeated and unsanctioned non-compliance with the Rules or orders as a denial of access to justice to the party delayed or denied resolution.
I agree.
This is a matter the case management judge may yet address in the upcoming contempt proceedings.
In Oommen v.
Capital Housing Corp., 2016 ABQB 283, 2016 CarswellAlta 903, 87 C.P.C.

(7th) 87, Justice Veit adopted the following principles relating to the imposition of sanctions for civil contempt: 37 The recent Crawford decision in Ontario usefully sets out some general principles concerning the sanctioning of civil contempt.
Although the decision deals specifically with family law proceedings, the principles apply to all areas of civil litigation.
192 In Cassidy v.
Cassidy, 2010 ONSC 2707, [2010] O.J.
No.

1927, the Court set out the following regarding sentencing in contempt proceedings: The sanction imposed upon a finding of contempt must be significant and of such consequence as to ensure the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute.
Sentencing in contempt proceedings, particular in family law proceedings, should be comprised of two components.
It should be restorative to the victim of the contempt and punitive to the contemnor.

To accomplish the former requires the sentence to correlate to the conduct that produces the contempt and to accomplish the latter requires the sentence not to reflect a marked departure from those imposed in like circumstances.
In determining an appropriate sentence in the present case, considerations include the following:

(a) The available sentences: For practical purposes the list of available penalties for civil contempt is a short one, consisting of: no penalty (where the contempt has been purged), a suspended sentence (perhaps conditional upon some act or event occurring), a fine, or incarceration.
(b) The proportionality of the sentence to the wrongdoing: A sentence, to be fit, must be proportionate to the gravity of the wrongdoing.
Although a finding of contempt carries with it the recognition that the conduct was deliberate and wilful, contempt can reflect degrees of wrongdoing.
All instances of contempt are serious, but some are more serious than others.
(c) The similarity of sentences in like circumstances: A sentence should not reflect a marked departure from those imposed in like circumstances.
Unfortunately, in the area of sentencing for contempt the reported and unreported decisions are scarce.
Those that do exist are heavily fact-driven.
While each case turns on its own facts, the general principles applied by the court are the same and the penalties differ, depending on the facts.
(d) The presence of mitigating factors: An admission of the facts by the contemnor may constitute a mitigating factor.
(e) The presence of aggravating factors: That the contemnor's conduct was flagrant and continued over a long period were aggravating factors.
(f) Deterrence: The primary purpose of sentencing in contempt proceedings, apart from coercing compliance, is deterrence: both general and specific.
The punishment for contempt should serve as a disincentive to those who might be included to breach court orders.
(g) The reasonableness of a fine: Where civil contempt is concerned, the ability to pay a fine is a crucial consideration in determining its size.
A small fine for a wealthy person is not a punishment.
Deterrence is not achieved unless fines are imposed in meaningful amounts.
A fine must be a punishment, not a nuisance.
Where a fine is imposed it must, in all of the circumstances, reflect the seriousness of the contempt.
(h) The reasonableness of incarceration: Incarceration is reasonable only where no other less restrictive sanction is appropriate.
It is appropriate in cases where there have been multiple breaches of court orders.
For any motion necessitated by contempt, the contemnor must pay the solicitor and client costs of the moving party.
193 In Boucher v.
Kennedy, [1998] O.J.
No.
1612 (C.J.) the following factors were considered when determining the appropriate sanctions:
(a) whether the contemnor had admitted the breach
(b) whether the contemnor has demonstrated a full acceptance of the paramountcy of the rule of law, by tendering a formal apology to the Court
(c) whether the breach was a single act or part of an ongoing pattern of conduct in which there were repeated breaches
(d) whether the breach occurred with the full knowledge and understanding of the contemnor that it was a breach rather than as a result of mistake or misunderstanding
(e) the extent to which the conduct of the contemnor displayed defiance
(f) whether the Order was a private one, affecting only the parties to the suit or whether some public benefit lay at the root of the Order
(g) the need for specific and general deterrence; and the ability of the contemnor to pay.
38 In our own province, in McDonald Estate (Re), Gates J. has summarized the principles in this way: 55 The Respondent refers to Michael v.
Lafrentz, [1998] A.J.
No.
1489, 1998 CarswellAlta 657 (CA) at paras.
31 and 32 and to Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel, [2005] A.J.
No.
662, 2005 CarswellAlta 739 (CA) at para.
12 for this list of factors to be taken into consideration in determining the penalty for contempt: 1.
Whether there was deliberate defiance of a Court order or whether there was an inadvertent failure to comply with the Court order; 2.
The role of legal counsel; 3.
Where there has been a failure to give discovery, the object of the exercise is more to secure the discovery rather than to punish; 4.
Attempts to purge contempt or to apologize are relevant; 5.
The entire context in the history of the litigation; 6.
The amount of reasonable thrown-away costs properly incurred; 7.
The nature of the contempt 8.
The degree of culpability of the contemnor.

Family Law Situations Many authorities go on to say that, family law situations should be treated as a special class of contempt, and that in those situations, jail should be the very last resort … With respect for those of that persuasion, I conclude that, without evidence on the point, a judge is not entitled to assume that a jail sentence is counter-productive in every family law contempt situation.

Because we think of family in terms of harmony and unity, it is perhaps counter-intuitive to expect that, for some types of contempt, and for some types of spouses or parents, a swift, sure jail sanction could, in the long run, prod family members towards greater harmony.
Yet, a judge could hear evidence that a firm stigmatizing of certain types of contempt can be in the best interests of both the family and of the public.
I adopt the more contemporary views on this issue as outlined by Beaulieu, J., in [Pilpel v.
Pilpel (1993), 27 C.P.C.
Gen.
Div.)].
In summary, contempt in family law situations should, in my view, be assessed like other forms of civil contempt: all aggravating and mitigating factors in the case must be considered.
S.
L.
217 (Q.B.), at 221, per Veit J.
In JLZ v.
CMZ, 2021 ABCA 200, 2021 CarswellAlta 1343, 27 Alta.
L.R.
(8th) 313, the court discussed the use of a change in parenting as a consequence of a finding of contempt.
[62] In summary, a change in parenting is available following a finding of contempt.
It should be used with restraint.
It must be proportionate to the gravity of the conduct and the personal culpability of the contemnor and the court must consider other, less drastic measures.
The overriding principle is whether the order is in the best interests of the child.

Two of the courts' fundamental obligations form the foundation of this case: the obligation to safeguard the dignity of the courts and the force of their orders, and the obligation to safeguard the best interests of children.
The primary mechanism by which the courts protect children is the making of orders.
A parent's wilful and repeated contempt of court orders may force the court to consider whether it can effectively maintain its parens patriae role while the children are in that parent's care.
In rare circumstances, a change of parenting might be necessary in service 4.
Suspended Sentences and Other Penalties In [Ansah v.
Ansah, [1977] 2 W.L.R.
760 (C.A.)], the British Court of Appeal made some useful comments about the technique of suspending sentence in civil contempt cases.
It described that technique as “dangerous”.

It continued: It would have been much safer to have adjourned the summons to commit with liberty to restore in the event of a further breach of the injunction or of a term imposed by the court at the first hearing of the summons.
S.
L.
217 (Q.B.), at 222, per Veit J.
However, in Dental Association (Alta.) v.
381 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Veit again considered “suspended sentences” and other penalties.
At pp.

Her counsel submitted that the earlier determinate sentence of 4 months' imprisonment (which had been served) rendered the Court functus and that the Court could impose no further sanction for the contempt.

The learned justice disagreed with defence counsel, and “held that the Court of Queen's Bench was not without jurisdiction to impose further sanctions with respect to ‘[Braun's] ongoing contempt regarding Orders of this Court.’” Ms.
Braun was found to still be in contempt, and was sentenced to another 4-month term of imprisonment (referred to by the Court of Appeal as “sixth Murray order”).
The March 11, 2005, order was the subject of this appeal.
Berger J.A., speaking for the panel, allowed the accused's appeal, and held that the lower court was functus when it imposed the sentence on March 11, 2005.
At pp.
26–27, his Lordship said: The gravamen of the analysis, I suggest, is to ascertain whether (using the criminal law analogy) the impugned act amounts to a new actus reus.
A person who is in possession of stolen property over a period of five days is not subject to prosecution for five offences.
On the other hand, five bank robberies will attract five charges.
The same is true of contempt.

Where there is a subsequent breach of a court order stemming from a positive act on the part of the contemnor, such as the breach of a restraining order or a breach of an injunction, the subsequent breach can found a second contempt charge resulting in further sanctions: Skeena Kraft Ltd. v.
Pulp & Paper Workers of Canada, supra, and U.N.A. v.
Alberta (Attorney General) (1990), 104 A.R.
246 (Alta.
C.A.); affirmed [1992] 1 S.C.R.
On the other hand, if an individual is ordered to attend examinations and wilfully fails to do so, the contempt crystallizes at the moment of non-compliance.
Like possession of stolen property, nonattendance the following day does not constitute a new actus reus.
If the contempt is not purged, the gravity of disobedience in the context of all of the circumstances is readily ascertained.

This includes an assessment of the contemnor's motives for non-compliance, the impact on interested third parties, the public nature of the contempt and its implications for the integrity of the administration of justice.
In such circumstances, one way of proceeding would be to adjourn once a finding of contempt is made and to schedule a sentencing hearing at some future date.
This would allow the contemnor to consider whether to purge her contempt.
If the contemnor elects to purge, that may be a mitigating factor.
If the contempt is not purged, continued disobedience is neither an aggravating feature nor a fresh transgression.
The sentence imposed should assume continued non-compliance.
The nature of the contempt will have been assessed and will have been the subject of judicial pronouncement and sanction.
Of course, it is always open to a contemnor to thereafter purge her contempt and to thereby mitigate the punishment that has been imposed.
The Court, in my opinion, retains jurisdiction to reduce a fine or a term of imprisonment already imposed when a contemnor later elects to comply with the Court's order.
The Court is not functus.
Rule 704(4) and the common law preserve the Court's ability, in appropriate circumstances, to vary or remit the sanction.
By proceeding in this fashion, respect for the administration of justice is enhanced, certainty is restored, and compliance with court orders is encouraged.
Of course, the present restrained and measured practices of the Courts will continue.
Judges who find a party to an action in civil contempt will almost always first consider non-penal sanctions such as the striking of pleadings and the imposition of costs.
That said, if a penal sanction such as imprisonment or a fine is imposed, the judicial arsenal is not thereby depleted.
The Court retains control over its own process and, if the unpurged contempt affects the fair adjudication of the suit, non-penal sanctions may still be invoked.

A civil contempt order has as its main purpose coercion—to promote compliance with a court's orders (Chiang at para 117
Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2017 ABQB 256 at paras 54, 82 [Demb ABQB 2017], aff'd 2017 ABCA 340 [Demb ABCA 2017], citing Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42 at para 59).
This power, however, is one that courts must use “cautiously and with great restraint” (Carey at para 36, citing TG Industries Ltd v Williams, 2001 NSCA 105 at para 32).
As such, a judge may decline to make a finding in contempt where the alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with a court order (Carey at para 37).

[33] However, it is also important to recognize that, as stated by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Knapp v Munro, 2015 ONSC 5444 at para 16: Notwithstanding the court's reluctance to exercise it contempt powers, it is important that such powers be exercised in appropriate cases to ensure that parties … understand that court orders cannot be ignored or disobeyed, and that compliance with a court order is neither an option nor a bargaining chip.
[34] A court assessing whether a party has purged their contempt should also consider the context of the original contempt order and the circumstances of the overarching litigation (see e.g.
Turkawski I
Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd, 2008 ABQB 27 at paras 4-5, 15 [Turkawski II]
Keephills Aggregate Co v Riverview Properties Inc., 2008 ABQB 540 at para 18 [Keephills]
Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5-6). … [37] It may be possible for a party found in contempt to purge their contempt without achieving perfect compliance with the order they previously breached.
This may be the case where the party shows that they are unable—as opposed to unwilling—to satisfy elements of the earlier order (Turkawski I at para 37; Turkawski II at para 15).

Additionally, the court may take into consideration that “the passage of time, and other factors, may affect the true importance of receiving complete satisfaction” of an earlier undertaking or requirement (Turkawski I at para 32).

The fact that a party has not achieved perfect compliance with an earlier requirement may be less important where the intended product of that requirement is no longer relevant (Turkawski I at para 53).

[38] Similarly, when document production is at the heart of the earlier contempt finding, a court may consider whether production has “run its course” at the time that a party applies to purge its contempt (Demb ABCA 2017 at para 6). … [45] The party seeking to purge its contempt holds the burden of showing that they have complied with the court order they previously breached or that despite their reasonable efforts, they are unable to do so: Turkawski I at para 37
Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at paras 24, 29.
It is not enough to show merely that any outstanding obligations are extremely difficult or onerous: Lymer (Re), 2017 ABQB 110 at para 27.
However, context is an important consideration: see e.g.
Turkawski I; Turkawski II at paras 4–5 15; Kee hills at para 18; Demb ABCA 2017 at paras 5–6

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.54 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) In this rule, (a) “examination” means a medical examination conducted for the purpose of determining a person's mental state; (b) “facility” means (i) a facility as defined in the Mental Health Act, or (ii) a correctional institution as defined in the Corrections Act. (2) If a person is declared to be in civil contempt of Court and the judge is satisfied that there are reasonable and probable grounds to believe that the person is (a) suffering from a mental disorder, or (b) likely to cause harm to himself or herself or others or to suffer substantial mental or physical deterioration or serious physical impairment, and would otherwise be unwilling, on that person's own initiative, to attend an examination, the judge may order that the person be taken into custody by a peace officer and taken to a facility for the purpose of examination and a report to the Court, as directed by the Court. (3) An order made under subrule (2) is sufficient authority to detain, control, transport, examine, care for, observe, assess and prepare a report for the Court about the person named in the order.

paragraphs.text: Nothing in these rules prevents or is to be interpreted as preventing the Court, as a superior court, from exercising its inherent power to cite in contempt and punish those who disobey the Court's lawful orders or who otherwise display contempt for its process.
